Question: Why is French spelling so irrational and unsystematic? Why don't they change it?
Answer: The French spelling is indeed irrational and unsystematic quite often. However, some spellings may seem irrational, but actually aren’t. Some examples of rational, but seemingly irrational spellings So many things, in the French language, can be explained by studying the history of it. You can also look at the “etymology”, which is the origin of the word. In French, a lot of words come from the latin, so some spellings are also explained by that. The final silent consonant are usually there for that reason. Some examples of irrational spellings Some spellings are however very artificial. One example of that would be “poids/pois/poix”. These words are spelled differently so we can make the difference between them. Another example would be the addition of “etymologic letters” so some words would appear more latin. At some point, many people wanted to protect latin, so they tried to make French appear more latin by adding some letters. I sadly don’t have any example coming at the top of my head. Why don’t we do anything about it? People are very conservative. In 1990, a reform was made in the French language. Some spellings were changed. The most famous word is “oignon”, that would now be written “ognon”, or “nénuphar”, that would now be written “nénufar”. Most people complained. The first reason, I believe, is that people learned some things and they didn’t want to unlearn them. The second reason is that many people think these modifications were the proof that we are getting dumber (“Kids can’t even learn French properly, we have to make it easier for them! Pfff!”). Another reason I heard, but quite rarely, was that many spellings, like I showed sooner, are explained by history and that by changing these spellings, we erase history. Strangely though, I often hear people saying: “French is so illogical!”, but then they also complain about the reform from 1990. Some have fair criticisms and I don’t pretend the reform is 100% good, but many complain about it without even knowing what it is. I know because I used to be one of these people, when I was much younger. ;) You have to know that French people are also usually very conservative. Recently, the idea of making French more “gender neutral” was discussed. In France, some people talked about having feminine forms for the words describing jobs. Many French people didn’t want to, they talked against it and really didn’t want an “avocat” (a lawyer) to be an “avocate” (a female lawyer) when the person is female, but in Québec, we have been doing that for years! In France, though, they don’t do that yet. You should also know that changing a language is very long. You can’t just learn something to people, then someday tell them: “Yo, we changed everything, so learn these new things now.” People definitely won’t.

Question: What languages are the hardest to learn as a new language? Is English considered an easy language to learn?
Answer: There are many things we must think about before answering this question. What is the speaker’s mother tongue? My native language is French, therefore learning Spanish, Catalan, Romanian or Italian are going to be easier for me than for an English speaker, for example, since they share similar roots. Grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation German has a fairly difficult grammar, but the pronunciation is very regular thus easy to learn. On the other side, English has a fairly easy grammar, but the pronunciation is very irregular thus harder to learn. You want an example? Pronounce “ear”, “heard” and “bear”. The letters “ear” aren’t pronounced the same way in any of these three words. What is the speaker’s access to the culture? The best way to learn a language is to immerse yourself in that language. An English learner will find plenty of things to read, watch or listen to since English has a huge cultural background. It’s pretty mainstream. However, let’s imagine I want to speak German. I don’t say the German cultural production is small or uninteresting, but as a Canadian, I have a smaller access to it. I must dig deeper to find it. Of course, some language are “objectively” easier or harder to learn than some (as an example, Spanish is, for most people, easier to learn than French), but when you ask which languages are harder to learn, this ain’t a question that can totally be answered without knowing some things about you beforehand.

Question: What does informal Québécois look like in contrast to informal French from France?
Answer: Both French and Québécois use anglicisms, but not the same. French people tend to use them more literally, and Québécois tend to “frenchify” them. As an example, in France, my friend asked where was the “salle the bain” (salle=room and bain=bath). The guy she asked it too wouldn’t understand, but at some point, he said: “Oh! Vous voulez dire bathroom!” (Oh! You mean the bathroom). It is not something only French people do, but maybe they do it more. In Québec, on the other hand, people transform a lot of English words, especially verbs. As an example, the word “to park (a car)” is used by Québécois, but we transform it a bit: “se parker”. We then conjugate it as a French verb: je me parke, tu te parkes, il se parke, etc. This is not something French people do, I believe. Another thing we do is that we translate English expression. In Québec, people say: “ça fait du sens”. It is the translation of “it makes sense”, because the French expression is actually “ça a du sens” (it has sense). Another example could be “faire face à la musique” (to face the music).

I mean… no offense, but I won’t learn Flemish because I was there for 3 days. Also, of course I’ll visit the main touristic attractions. The Eiffel tower? Check. The Manneken-Pis? Check. I have a friend who didn’t want to visit these places when she travelled because they were “so touristic”. Too bad for you, they’re usually popular for a reason. Most of them were great (okay, the Manneken-Pis wasn’t haha). Plus, they are symbols. They’re kind of a reality check: “Yep, you’re truly in Paris, look, here is the Eiffel tower!” “Guided tours are so touristic!” Well, I love them (not too many though), especially the ones in which you get to walk around for a couple hours and use the public transportations. They lead me to places I would have looked at and not really cared about. Now, I have a guide to explain to me why that place is interesting and its history! Plus they usually have good adresses for restaurants and bars (never been disappointed listening to their advices). I also read about how going to Mc Donald’s is touristic. But… I like going to Mc Donald’s to see the differences in the menu since Mc Donald’s adapts it to the cultures. To me, it is a cultural experience actually. ;) I do all these things, but I always end up trying the local cuisine too, speaking with locals, going to shows, sport events, theater, etc. So my travels weren’t less interesting nonetheless. I still lived an adventure, I still got in touch with the locals, I still got lost, I still admired the beauty… even though I took selfies! So what is the difference between a tourist and a traveller? To me, there are none. Each one get to experiment his/her trip the way he/she wants and is pleased and no judgement should be made (except if that person is an arsehole, of course). It doesn’t mean the trip was less of an adventure. It doesn’t mean you don’t get to discover the culture. You’re a traveller even though you sleep in a bed or get in a cab vs sleep in a tent and do hitchhiking. I’m not a fan of doing what I’m about to do, but the dictionnary makes no difference between both of these words. At least, not the ones I looked at. By definition, being in a new country is by default being a tourist. I’m a big fan of that definition. To be fair, most answers here seemed very condescending to me. Some were also utterly confusing to me.

Question: In the perfect horror story, how would an inhuman thing be portrayed to be the most scary to you?
Answer: In that answer, there are spoilers about the first issues of The Walking Dead comic books. My answer is a bit similar to Luuk Schuring’s one. First of all, it wouldn’t be physically disgusting. I like horror, but I dislike most scary movies because of that reason: they usually rely on visual horror. Visual horror is not scary, it’s disgusting. Disgust and fear are two different emotions. There is a quote from Stephen King that I like very much because it explains it all: The 3 types of terror The Gross-out: the sight of a severed head tumbling down a flight of stairs, it's when the lights go out and something green and slimy splatters against your arm. The Horror: the unnatural, spiders the size of bears, the dead waking up and walking around, it's when the lights go out and something with claws grabs you by the arm. And the last and worse one: Terror, when you come home and notice everything you own had been taken away and replaced by an exact substitute. It's when the lights go out and you feel something behind you, you hear it, you feel its breath against your ear, but when you turn around, there's nothing there... Based on that, there are two examples I know that got it right. Slenderman: the eight pages In that game, you control a woman who is alone in a park, unarmed. It’s dark and the only light comes from the moon and a flashlight you’re holding. The goal is very simple: you must find eight page (pinned on walls or trees) before Slenderman, who chases you, finds you. Here is our gentleman. As you can see, he does look strange, but is he disgusting? Not at all. He’s actually quite fancy with his suit. So back to the game. When Slenderman is close, the screen gets blurred. You then have a little bit of time to get away. He won’t move. He’ll simply stare at you. Here is a video of the game if you haven’t played it yet. This one is very funny to be fair haha! Oh, and here is the thing. I have never completed the game, but I heard that once you get the eight pages, you can’t get away. The only thing you can do is wandering around until Slenderman catches you. There is no escape. It follows I haven’t seen this movie yet, but I read a bit about it. The story is about a “supernatural STD” (that actually sounds very scary). When you catch it, you are chase by an entity. You can get rid of it by having sex with someone else, but if that person dies, it will get back at you. And maybe you won’t know that this person died, so you can never be sure who has it now. You’d probably lose the track of it after a while. Maybe it’ll get back at you in like… 20 years. You’re never truly safe. It’s never truly gone. The conclusion So what do the entities showed in the two examples have in common? A last example: The Walking Dead The zombies from the first The Walking Dead comic books are also good examples. At the beginning, when the horror relied mostly on zombies, that feeling of paranoia and never being safe was portrayed a lot. As an example, Donna wasn’t careful for a second and for that reason, she got eaten. It shows that you’re never safe. It was a bright day, she was with other people, talking with her husband one minute ago… and then she died. It was quite a gruesome death. The same thing happened to Amy. She was with her friend, cracking some jokes and then - pouf - she’s dead. Zombies are disgusting though.

Question: What are some ways to swear in French?
Answer: It depends of where you are. In France, the most common words are “merde”, “putain” and “bordel”. However, in Quebec, we don’t use these often. Our swearwords come from the religious vocabulary. The most common ones are “criss” (christ), “calice” (chalice), “ostie” (host) et “tabarnaque” (tabernacle). We use them as nouns, verbs, adjectives, etc. As an example, here is a sentence: Mon petit criss (noun), je vais t’en calicer (verb) une tabarnaque (noun). Tu vas t’en souvenir crissement (adverb) longtemps. It means something like: “You basterd, I’ll punch you in the face. You’ll remember it for a long time.”

Question: Is Quebec culturally closer to France or to the rest of Canada?
Answer: It’s a hard question and I’m sorry since I’ll use some stereotypes to answer it. Here is a map showing the results of the 2011 federal elections. The blue provinces are the one who mainly voted for the Conservative party. As you can see, Québec’s results are different to most Canadian provinces ones. English Canadians are usually more “conservative” than Québécois. I must say though that it seems that English Canadians are more open to multiculturalism than Québécois, but the thing is they don’t worry about the disparition of their language, unlike Québécois (I don’t want to excuse the fact some Québécois choose to be racist as a defense mecanism though). So, France and Québec are closer then, you’ll tell me. Well, I’m not quite sure either. Like French people, Québécois are usually quite “direct”, but we’re also usually more polite than them, so I would say we’re somewhere between English Canadians and French for that. Men-women love relationships are a mix of both too. We’re more “wild” than English Canadians, but we’re also much more equal/feminist than French. So yet again, it’s a tie. For the language, it’s quite simple: we’re more French. Although Québécois French and French from France are somehow different, it’s still the same language and we’re able to communicate. Culturally speaking, I learned more about France than about Canada’s history in high school. And in cégep (it’s after high school), every students must complete two French literature classes. I actually know almost nothing about English Canada history. Also, for English Canadians, as an example, John McDonald is one of Canada “founders”, but he was elected in 1867, 260 years after Quebec city foundation, so it’s very weird for us to consider him as such. To Québécois, this year “Canada’s 150th anniversary celebrations” were quite strange (we celebrated “Quebec city 400th anniversary” almost 10 years ago and “Montreal 375th anniversary this year). But now, let’s talk about snow. Of course, for this one, we’re much more closer to English Canadians. It’s quite a running joke in Québec when we see that it snowed in France and they can’t deal with it properly (but we understand why it’s hard for them). And hockey. Jeez. I hate hockey, but people here like it so much. As much as English Canadians. So we’re really a mix of both, but it is also too simplistic to simply answer that. Québec also has its own cultural background: its own variety of French, its own cuisine (poutine, maple syrup, tourtière, pea soup, apple ice cider, etc.), its own culture (movies, music, literature…), etc. I don’t want to sound like I hate English Canadians by the way. I hope it didn’t sound this way. But to be honest, English Canada feels like another country to me, just like France. Not a country I hate, just a country that is different from where I live. Québec situation is a very strange one.

Question: How mutually intelligible are French from France, and Canadian French?
Answer: Wow, after I read the other answers, I feel like I have to put my two cents. I talked with French people multiple times. Like maybe a hundred. Probably even more. And NEVER did they tell me they couldn’t understand me. They told me I have a funny (or a beautiful) accent, yes. Sometimes, I used a word they did not understand. But they clearly understood like 98% of what I told them. And when I visited France (twice), people would always be able to identify me very easily as a Québécoise (sometimes I only said a few words). So I was clearly speaking “Canadian French”. I recently wrote an answer about why Canadian French can be hard to understand for some people: Quelqu'un's answer to Why is it that Canadian French is so incomprehensible to the ears of a European? The problem is not the variety of French, it’s the register. That’s also why French French, Swiss French, Belgian French… these can all be hard to understand when the speaker use the casual register. A Marseillais once told me: “C’est complètement fada!” I had never heard that word before. He told me this is a word only used in South of France. I later looked in the dictionary. Guess what: it’s from the casual register. French from France and Canada are very much intelligible when speakers are aware of their differences.
